body:
Ambedkar's place in the national movement

Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was a jurist, political leader, economist and major advocate of the rights of people subjected to untouchability and caste discrimination. His central contribution was to insist that political freedom should be accompanied by social equality, human dignity and effective political representation.

Ambedkar's experiences of caste discrimination helped shape his opposition to the denial of education, access to public facilities and equal civic rights. His activities included organising disadvantaged communities, leading public protests and seeking constitutional safeguards.

Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha: 1924

On 20 July 1924, the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha was established in Bombay. Ambedkar was central to its organisation and served as chairman of its managing committee.

The Sabha sought to improve education, social conditions and economic opportunities for the Depressed Classes and to represent their grievances before public authorities. It reflected Ambedkar's belief that oppressed communities needed organised collective action as well as legal protection.

Mahad Satyagraha: 1927

In March 1927, Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha in present-day Maharashtra. Its immediate issue was the right of people treated as untouchable to draw water from the public Chavdar Tank.

The struggle challenged the belief that caste status could determine who was entitled to use a public source of water. It was therefore a movement for equal civic rights, not merely a protest about a shortage of drinking water.

Kalaram Temple Entry Movement: 1930

In 1930, Ambedkar launched a temple-entry struggle associated with the Kalaram Temple at Nashik. The movement challenged the exclusion of Dalits from religious spaces on the basis of caste.

Mahad and Kalaram should be distinguished by their immediate objectives: Mahad concerned access to public water, while Kalaram concerned temple entry. Both were part of the larger movement against untouchability.

Political representation and the Poona Pact

Ambedkar argued that social equality required political safeguards. At the Round Table Conferences, he supported separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, under which voters from that community would elect their own representatives.

Gandhi opposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes because he believed they would deepen political separation within Hindu society. The disagreement resulted in the Poona Pact of September 1932.

The Pact provided for reserved seats for the Depressed Classes within a joint electorate, rather than the proposed separate electorates. In a joint electorate, representatives for reserved seats are ultimately elected by the wider constituency electorate, not exclusively by voters from the reserved community.

Remember the distinction

The Poona Pact did not abolish reserved representation. It replaced the proposed separate-electorate arrangement with reserved seats under joint electorates.

Ambedkar and the Constitution of India

After independence, Ambedkar became India's first Law Minister in 1947. He was also appointed chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, constituted on 29 August 1947.

The Drafting Committee prepared the constitutional text for consideration by the Constituent Assembly. Ambedkar played a central role in presenting and explaining the draft, but the Constitution was the result of a wider collective process involving the Assembly and its committees.

His work on social justice and constitutional safeguards helped connect the struggle for dignity with the institutions of independent India.

Prelims focus

  • Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha: 20 July 1924, Bombay.
  • Mahad Satyagraha: Chavdar Tank, 1927.
  • Kalaram Temple Entry Movement: Nashik, 1930.
  • Poona Pact: September 1932.
  • Drafting Committee: constituted on 29 August 1947; chaired by Ambedkar.
  • Trap: Mahad was associated with public water access; the Kalaram struggle concerned temple entry.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 103–105; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Chapter 3, section The Limits of Civil Disobedience, printed pp. 67–68; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Volume 17, Part II, section Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha; Dr. Ambedkar Foundation, About Dr. Ambedkar, sections on Mahad and Kalaram; Constituent Assembly Debates, proceedings of 29 August 1947. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: B. R. Ambedkar: Social Equality, Political Representation and the Constitution

body:
Why social reform formed part of the national awakening

The struggle against colonial rule developed alongside movements opposing caste discrimination, restrictions on women's education and unequal social customs. Social reformers argued that a society seeking freedom also needed to examine inequalities within its own institutions.

These reform movements were not identical to the political activities of the Congress. Some reformers criticised nationalist organisations when they believed those organisations paid insufficient attention to caste or gender inequality.

Jyotirao Phule: Opposition to caste inequality

Jyotirao Phule, also known as Jyotiba Phule, opposed the social dominance of upper castes and argued for the dignity and equality of oppressed communities.

In 1873, he founded the Satyashodhak Samaj, or Society of Truth Seekers. The organisation challenged caste hierarchy and promoted social equality.

Phule also wrote Gulamgiri in 1873. The title means slavery. He drew attention to similarities between caste oppression in India and the denial of freedom experienced by enslaved people elsewhere.

Savitribai Phule: Women's education

Savitribai Phule was a pioneering advocate of women's education and worked closely with Jyotirao Phule. They established a school for girls at Pune in 1848.

Her contribution illustrates an important point: education was not only a means of acquiring knowledge but also a way of challenging restrictions that prevented women and marginalised communities from participating equally in society.

Periyar and the Self-Respect Movement

E. V. Ramasamy Naicker, popularly known as Periyar, was a major social reformer associated with southern India. He challenged caste privilege, religiously justified inequality and the inferior social position assigned to women.

Periyar launched the Self-Respect Movement, which promoted dignity, rational criticism of discriminatory customs and equality in social relationships. He had participated in the Congress but later criticised the persistence of caste distinctions within nationalist society.

Periyar's principal field was social reform and the struggle against caste hierarchy. This distinguishes him from a leader whose main achievement was organising a particular anti-British political campaign.

Other reformers and their institutions

ReformerInstitution or actionMain contribution
Raja Rammohun RoyBrahmo Sabha; campaign against satiWomen's rights and social reform
Ishwarchandra VidyasagarCampaign supporting widow remarriage; law enacted in 1856Widow remarriage and girls' education
Swami Dayanand SaraswatiArya Samaj, 1875Religious and social reform
Jyotirao PhuleSatyashodhak Samaj, 1873Opposition to caste inequality
Savitribai PhuleGirls' education at Pune, 1848Women's education and equality
PeriyarSelf-Respect MovementAnti-caste reform and social dignity

How these contributions relate to Ambedkar

Phule and Periyar challenged caste inequality through social organisation and criticism of discriminatory practices. Ambedkar also fought caste discrimination, but placed particular emphasis on legal rights, political representation and constitutional safeguards.

The movements therefore shared a concern for equality while differing in the institutions they created and the remedies they emphasised.

Prelims focus

  • Jyotirao Phule: Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873.
  • Gulamgiri: Jyotirao Phule, 1873.
  • Savitribai Phule: pioneering work in girls' education at Pune.
  • Periyar: Self-Respect Movement.
  • Dayanand Saraswati: Arya Samaj, 1875.
  • Trap: Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by Jyotirao Phule, not B. R. Ambedkar.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 96–107, particularly sections Gulamgiri and The Non-Brahman Movement; Government of India, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Unsung Heroes of Freedom Movement, entry Periyar E. V. Ramasamy. Online source consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Important social reformers and the inequalities they challenged.

title: Social Reform Leaders: Phule, Savitribai Phule, Periyar and Equality

body:
Bose's political outlook

Subhas Chandra Bose, widely known as Netaji, was a leading nationalist who believed that British rule had to be ended through determined political action. He supported strong national organisation, economic planning and a more militant approach to the struggle for independence.

Bose admired Gandhi's contribution to national awakening but disagreed with the view that non-violence should be the only method used to secure freedom.

Congress President at Haripura: 1938

Bose presided over the Haripura session of the Indian National Congress in 1938. Haripura is in Gujarat, giving the session special significance in the history of the national movement within the state.

Bose was again elected Congress President in 1939, when the Congress met at Tripuri. Political differences with Gandhi's supporters and sections of the Congress leadership resulted in his resignation from the presidency.

In 1939, Bose formed the Forward Bloc to organise supporters of a more assertive nationalist programme.

The Indian National Army: First organisation and later leadership

The Indian National Army (INA), also known as the Azad Hind Fauj, was organised among Indians in Southeast Asia during the Second World War.

An important historical distinction is that the INA had been organised under Captain Mohan Singh in 1942, before Bose assumed leadership of the movement in Southeast Asia. Rash Behari Bose was associated with the Indian Independence League and helped prepare the way for Subhas Chandra Bose's leadership.

Subhas Chandra Bose took over the leadership of the movement in 1943 and reorganised the INA as a force seeking India's independence from British rule.

Mohan Singh: Early INA organisation in 1942.
Rash Behari Bose: Indian Independence League and transfer of leadership.
Subhas Chandra Bose: Leadership and reorganisation of the INA from 1943.

Provisional Government of Azad Hind: 1943

On 21 October 1943, Bose proclaimed the Provisional Government of Azad Hind in Singapore. It represented an attempt to establish a government committed to India's liberation from British rule.

In 1944, the INA participated in the military campaign towards India's northeastern frontier, associated particularly with Imphal and Kohima. The campaign failed to achieve its objective.

Later, the trials of INA personnel generated widespread public sympathy and nationalist mobilisation. The INA is therefore remembered both for its military campaign and for its political impact on public opinion.

Bose and Bhagat Singh: Two distinct associations

Bhagat Singh was associated with revolutionary nationalism and the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA), reorganised under that name in 1928. His activities belonged to an earlier phase of revolutionary struggle.

Bose, by contrast, is particularly associated with Congress leadership in 1938–1939 and the INA in 1943–1945. Both supported independence, but their organisations and principal periods of activity were different.

Prelims focus

  • Haripura Congress session: Bose, 1938, Gujarat.
  • Tripuri Congress session: Bose, 1939.
  • Forward Bloc: formed by Bose in 1939.
  • Early INA organisation: Captain Mohan Singh, 1942.
  • Provisional Government of Azad Hind: 21 October 1943, Singapore.
  • Trap: Bose led and reorganised the INA in 1943; he was not the founder of its original 1942 organisation.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, section Bose and the INA, printed p. 123; Indian National Congress, Brief History of Congress, 1935–1945, Haripura and Tripuri entries; Indian National Congress, Subhas Chandra Bose as Congress President; Ministry of Home Affairs, historical movement listing, entry Indian National Army and Indian Independence League, 1942–1946; UK National Archives, Subhas Chandra Bose and India at War, section on the INA in 1943. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline from Bose's Congress presidency to the INA, distinguishing Mohan Singh's organisation in 1942 from Bose's leadership in 1943.
pictures.caption: Bose's principal political and military milestones.

title: Subhas Chandra Bose: Congress Leadership, the INA and Armed Resistance

body:
A major nationalist leader of the frontier region

Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan was a Pashtun leader from the North-West Frontier Province of British India. He is also known as Badshah Khan and the Frontier Gandhi.

His principal contribution was organising a disciplined movement of non-violent resistance among the Pashtun population. This is significant because the movement developed in a frontier region where political life was shaped by strong traditions of tribal organisation and frequent colonial repression.

Khudai Khidmatgar: 1929

In 1929, Ghaffar Khan established the Khudai Khidmatgar Movement. The name means Servants of God. Its members became widely known as the Red Shirts because of their distinctive clothing.

The organisation encouraged public service, education, social reform and disciplined non-violent action against British rule. Members were expected to avoid violence and revenge.

Khudai Khidmatgar = Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan = North-West Frontier Province = Red Shirts = Non-violent resistance.

Connection with Gandhi and the Congress

Ghaffar Khan's movement developed a close association with Gandhi and the Indian National Congress. Both Gandhi and Ghaffar Khan believed that disciplined non-violence could become an effective form of political resistance.

In 1930, the frontier region became a major centre of civil resistance. The repression of protesters at Qissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar became an important event in the history of the movement.

The Khudai Khidmatgars demonstrated that non-violent anti-colonial mobilisation was not confined to Gujarat, Bengal or other better-known centres of Congress activity.

Position on the Partition of India

Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan strongly opposed the Partition of India in 1947. He disagreed with the acceptance of partition by the Congress leadership.

His opposition is an important part of his political identity. He supported freedom from British rule but did not consider the division of India a desirable outcome.

Distinguishing Ghaffar Khan from Subhas Chandra Bose

Both were important opponents of colonial rule, but their most characteristic organisations followed different methods.

  • Ghaffar Khan: Khudai Khidmatgar, non-violent service and resistance, North-West Frontier Province.
  • Subhas Chandra Bose: Indian National Army, armed anti-colonial campaign, Southeast Asia.

The common surname Khan should not cause confusion with other leaders of the freedom movement. The distinctive institutional association is Khudai Khidmatgar.

Prelims focus

  • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan: Frontier Gandhi and Badshah Khan.
  • Khudai Khidmatgar Movement: established in 1929.
  • Khudai Khidmatgar members: Red Shirts.
  • Principal region: North-West Frontier Province.
  • Ghaffar Khan opposed the Partition of India in 1947.
  • Trap: The Red Shirts were associated with non-violent resistance, not with the Indian National Army.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, Towards Independence and Partition, printed p. 125; International Center on Nonviolent Conflict, The Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) Movement: Badshah Khan and the Northwest Frontier in British India, historical background and movement sections; Maharashtra State Board for Literature and Culture, India Fights for Freedom, section on the Frontier Province and the Red Shirts. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Founded in 1929 by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the Red Shirts linked education and service with disciplined non-violence in anti-British resistance.
pictures.caption: The principles and objectives of the Khudai Khidmatgar Movement.

title: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan: The Khudai Khidmatgar Movement
